verdicts.trueWording: where a more modern work looks back upon and refashions particular elements
verdicts.note: Raw article (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) line: "Martin's expansive lands ... are, in point of fact, what we call 'medievalism,' where a more modern work looks back upon and refashions particular elements of the Middle Ages into a new imaginative construction." Byline 'By Michael Livingston'. The ASOIAF limb is carried by the article body (A Song of Ice and Fire named four times) and by Livingston's own on-page comment: "'medievalism' (which is what Knight's Tale, ASOIF, and so many other wonderful works are)".

verdicts.trueWording: A good editor tries to figure out what the writer was trying to do
verdicts.note: Raw speech page (HTTP 200), header 'Guest of Honor Speech / Delivered at Coastcon II / March 10, 1979'. Full sentence: "A good editor tries to figure out what the writer was trying to do, and helps him or her do it better, rather than trying to change the book into something else entirely." Every limb present; the claim's 'helps him' compresses the page's 'helps him or her'.

verdicts.trueWording: Ultimately a writer lives or dies by his words
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: "Ultimately a writer lives or dies by his words, and he must always have the last word if his work is to retain its integrity." Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Or - horror of horrors - make the changes without bothering to inform the writer
verdicts.note: Page: "The worst of them insist. Or - horror of horrors - make the changes without bothering to inform the writer." The condemnation limb is carried by 'the worst of them' and 'horror of horrors', and reinforced by "A good editor doesn't insist, or make changes without permission."

verdicts.trueWording: He liked it even less, called it a "travelog."
verdicts.note: Page names the editor in full at first mention: "there was an editor in the field named Robert Hoskins." Anecdote: "So I sent him another story, quickly, and that one came back too. He liked it even less, called it a 'travelog.' ... The title was 'With Morning Comes Mistfall.'" All three limbs (Hoskins, rejection, travelog, the named story) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a short, polite note that said it was "eloquent," but not a story
verdicts.note: Page: "I sent him yet another. It returned with a short, polite note that said it was 'eloquent,' but not a story." Within the Hoskins sequence, so the 'Hoskins returned' limb is supported by context.

verdicts.trueWording: "You have a facile way with words," he said in summation
verdicts.note: Page: "Hoskins returned it almost sadly, with a long letter. ... 'You have a facile way with words,' he said in summation. 'As yet, you haven't convinced me that your words will strike sparks with readers.'" Speaker attribution to Hoskins is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: But it is a pseudo history of sorts, by an in world character
verdicts.note: Raw transcript (HTTP 200; page dated August 25, 2022, opening line 'On August 18, 2022, we interviewed George RR Martin in person'). Martin: "But it was not a traditional novel. It was a, I called it fake history at first. ... But it is a pseudo history of sorts, by an in world character." The Fire & Blood referent is explicit in the same exchange ('in Blood and Fire, of course' and later 'So I thought it would be fun to do that in Fire and Blood').

verdicts.trueWording: I called it fake history at first ... so I started calling it imaginary history
verdicts.note: Same sentence run: "I called it fake history at first. And then some of my readers said they hated that term, so I started calling it imaginary history." Both the first-term and the switch-after-readers-hated-it limbs are verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Why don't I give all versions? Cause history is uncertain.
verdicts.note: Page: "So I thought it would be fun to do that in Fire and Blood. ... And then at some point it hit me. Why don't I give all versions? Cause history is uncertain. I'll give all versions and it'll be fun for me." Fire & Blood referent explicit four paragraphs above the quote.

verdicts.trueWording: In Fire and Blood, I didn't have to have to make up my mind
verdicts.note: Page sets the contrast first: "When I get to a chapter in The Winds of Winter and I know something's gonna happen. How does it happen? ... I have to make up up my mind. In Fire and Blood, I didn't have to have to make up my mind." The Winds of Winter chapter limb is supported verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: I love history, but it's so unreliable to know what actually happened
verdicts.note: Page, closing the New York World building research anecdote: "That really impressed on me... that history... I love history, but it's so unreliable to know what actually happened." The 'researching the New York World building' limb is the anecdote it directly concludes.

verdicts.trueWording: It had 15 stories. ... This other book, 14. ... one book that had 20 stories
verdicts.note: Page: "It had 15 stories. Now, wait a minute. This other book, 14. 14, 15. And then I encountered one book that had 20 stories. What??? ... And I can't even find a reputable source as to how many floors it had." All three figures (14, 15, 20) and the disagreeing-sources limb are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: I did wanna make the Nightfort a sinister place, with its own legends
verdicts.note: Page, answering Aziz's question about the Nightfort scene with Bran and the Moria homage: "I did wanna make the Nightfort a sinister place, with its own legends." Verbatim, both limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: I turn it up to 11 or I turn it up to 111. Cause you don't ever wanna make it smaller.
verdicts.note: Page: "if I'm picking on something for history, to adapt to it, as I've often said in interviews, I turn it up to 11 or I turn it up to 111. Cause you don't ever wanna make it smaller. ... No, you have to make it bigger and cooler." The adaptation limb is explicit in the preceding sentence.
